title: Find which of our methods fills the young generation

blocks.text: The export service collects young garbage every few hundred milliseconds, and the team has a Flight Recorder file from production to find out why. Nobody wants to read four thousand events by hand. We want a small report: for one thread, how many bytes each of our own methods allocated, so that the first line names code we can change.

`AllocationReport` already reads the recording, keeps the `jdk.ObjectAllocationSample` events of the thread you ask for, and adds up a number per method. Finish the two `TODO`s in `src/main/java/practice/AllocationReport.java`:

items: `allocatingMethod(frames, appPackage)`: which of the application's methods a sample is charged to, as `"class.method"`;
`bytes(sample)`: how many bytes the sample accounts for.

blocks.text: When you're done, the numbers in the report add up to roughly what the thread allocated, and every entry is a method of the application that allocated, not one of the JDK's and not the method the thread happened to start in. About six lines in total.

The tests make a real recording of a worker that builds CSV files and SVG badges, and compare the report with the thread's own allocation counter. The `jdk.jfr.consumer` javadoc lists what an event and a frame can tell you.

cases.says: the report has entries for a thread that allocated during the recording and none for a thread that only waited
the bytes in the report add up to within half of what the thread really allocated
every method in the report belongs to the application, none to the JDK
allocations are charged to the application method closest to them, not to the method the thread started in

origin.section: A JFR Allocation Sample Stands for All the Bytes Since the Previous One

concepts: An allocation sample's top frame is usually the JDK's allocation helper; the application method responsible is the first of its frames further down the stack.
A jdk.ObjectAllocationSample's weight is what its thread allocated since its previous sample, so summing weights estimates allocated bytes, and counting samples does not.
